lesson.title: Head-On Overlap: The Sigma Bond Every Bond Has
lesson.summary: A sigma bond forms from the direct, head-on overlap of two orbitals along the line connecting their nuclei, and it is the one bond that every single, double, and triple covalent bond always contains.
lesson.body:
A sigma, or σ, bond forms when two orbitals overlap head on, directly along the imaginary line connecting the two bonded nuclei. This overlap puts the shared electron density squarely on and around that internuclear axis, giving sigma bonds a shape that is symmetric all the way around the bond axis, like a cylinder wrapped around the line between the two atoms. This head on geometry is the strongest, most direct kind of orbital overlap, which is why sigma bonds are generally the strongest single type of covalent bond.

Sigma bonds can form from several different combinations of orbitals, and the hybridization concepts already covered supply most of them. Two hydrogen 1s orbitals overlapping head on form the sigma bond in H2. An sp3 hybrid orbital on carbon overlapping with a hydrogen 1s orbital forms each C-H sigma bond in methane. Two sp3 hybrid orbitals overlapping with each other form the C-C sigma bond in ethane. The same pattern extends to sp2 and sp hybrid orbitals: whatever hybrid orbitals a bonded atom is using, their head on overlap with a partner orbital produces a sigma bond. Sigma bonds do not strictly require hybrid orbitals either; two unhybridized p orbitals pointed directly at each other along the internuclear axis, as in the F-F bond of F2, also overlap head on to form a perfectly ordinary sigma bond. What defines a sigma bond is always the head on geometry of the overlap, not which specific type of orbital happens to be involved.

One rule ties sigma bonds directly to the bond types you already draw in Lewis structures: every single covalent bond is exactly one sigma bond, and no more. Every double bond and every triple bond also contains exactly one sigma bond as its foundation, with additional pi bonds layered on top to account for the second and third bond in those structures, a relationship developed fully in the next concept.

The cylindrical symmetry of a sigma bond has a direct physical consequence: the two atoms it connects can rotate around the bond axis without disturbing the overlap at all, because the overlapping electron density is evenly distributed all the way around that axis regardless of rotation angle. Ethane's C-C sigma bond is the standard example. The two CH3 groups at either end of ethane can spin freely relative to each other, passing through many different rotational arrangements called conformations, without ever breaking the sp3 to sp3 orbital overlap that holds the molecule together.

This free rotation is not automatic for every bond, only for bonds that are purely sigma with nothing else layered on top. As soon as a pi bond joins a sigma bond to form a double or triple bond, that freedom disappears, because pi bonds rely on a very different, side by side kind of overlap that breaks apart if the atoms twist. Understanding exactly why that happens, and what a pi bond looks like, is the natural next step after sigma bonds.
